passage:
Papa was calling from the ship, and the network kept cutting out, so Kunal, nine, had only two minutes. "Tell me about your week, champ!"
Kunal gripped the phone. "Today Jaiswal sir made us stand outside for talking. He's the worst teacher."
His mother Hansa, sitting beside him, raised her eyebrows. On Monday Kunal had come home glowing because Jaiswal sir let him run the science experiment. On Wednesday he'd scored full marks in spelling. His big sister Arohi mouthed, "Tell him about the rocket!"
"Oh, and... um." Kunal frowned, trying to remember. The line crackled. "Standing outside was really bad, Papa."
The call dropped. Hansa smiled. "Next call, we'll make a list first."

qa.q: What happened at school today, according to Kunal?
qa.a: Jaiswal sir made them stand outside for talking.

qa.q: Why does Kunal call Jaiswal sir "the worst teacher"?
qa.a: Kunal feels upset about today's punishment, and because it is freshest in his mind it crowds out Monday's experiment, so the latest class seems like the whole truth about the teacher.

qa.q: How could Hansa's list idea help on the next call?
qa.a: Writing down something from each day before the call helps Kunal remember Monday and Wednesday, not only the last day.

qa.q: What might Papa think of Jaiswal sir after this call?
qa.a: Papa might think the teacher is harsh, without knowing Kunal loved running the science experiment earlier in the week.

grounding: It shows a boy, on a short phone call, describing his week only by the last day and judging a teacher by the latest class.

passage:
In their flat in Munirka, Delhi, Mawia's big sister Lalremsiami was filling in the school's weekly feedback form for him. "Which day of the week did you like best?"
"Friday," Mawia, eight, said at once. "We had the magic show."
"What about Tuesday? You went to the zoo! You talked about the tiger for hours."
Mawia scrunched his face. "Oh yeah. The tiger."
"And your teacher, Damini ma'am? Good or not good?"
"Not good. Yesterday she gave us extra homework."
"She also gave you a star for your poem on Wednesday."
"Did she?" Mawia genuinely couldn't remember.
Lalremsiami laughed and wrote "Friday" and "Tuesday" side by side.

qa.q: Where did Mawia go on Tuesday?
qa.a: The zoo.

qa.q: Why does Mawia rate Damini ma'am "not good"?
qa.a: Mawia still feels annoyed about the extra homework yesterday, the freshest thing he remembers about her, so it outweighs the star she gave him on Wednesday.

qa.q: How could the feedback form be filled in more fairly?
qa.a: Go through the week day by day with Mawia, as his sister started doing, before choosing a favourite day or judging the teacher.

qa.q: How might Damini ma'am feel reading "not good" because of one homework day?
qa.a: She might feel it's unfair, since earlier in the week she praised his poem with a star.

grounding: It shows a boy recalling mostly yesterday when asked about his week and judging his teacher by the last class.

passage:
"Faiz, how was your week?" his mother Farida asked, stirring the dal.
"Bad."
"Bad? All of it?"
"Deepika miss shouted at the whole class today because Nabeel threw chalk."
"And Monday?"
"Monday..." Faiz thought. "Monday was sports."
"Didn't you win the sack race on Monday?"
"Oh. Yes! I came first."
"And Wednesday?"
"Wednesday Deepika miss let me read my story to the class." He looked surprised. "She said it was the best one."
"So was it a bad week?"
Faiz dipped a finger in the dal and licked it. "Today was bad."
"Today was bad," Ammi agreed. "And the rest?"
"The rest was actually good."

qa.q: What did Faiz win on Monday?
qa.a: The sack race; he came first.

qa.q: Why does Faiz first say his whole week was bad?
qa.a: Faiz feels upset about today's shouting, the most recent and loudest memory, so it colours the whole week until his mother reminds him of earlier days.

qa.q: How did Farida help Faiz see the week differently?
qa.a: She walked him back through Monday and Wednesday with questions, letting him remember the sack race and the story himself. 😊

qa.q: How might Deepika miss feel if she knew Faiz first called the week bad?
qa.a: She might be surprised, since on Wednesday she praised his story as the best one.

grounding: It shows a boy judging his whole week and his teacher by what happened today, until earlier days are recalled.

passage:
I'm Pankaj, and when I was nine, Uma Nani would ring every Sunday and say, "Tell me your whole week, my boy."
One Sunday I said, "Bad week. The new maths teacher is mean." Nani asked why. "Yesterday she took my eraser away because I was playing with it."
Nani asked, "And on Monday?"
I had to think hard. On Monday the same teacher had stayed back to help me with fractions and said I was quick. On Wednesday we had the kite-making class. On Thursday I scored a goal.
But all I could feel was Saturday. It was like the other days had been rubbed out.
Nani laughed and said, "One eraser and the whole week is gone?" I laughed too. But I still told Papa the teacher was mean.

qa.q: Why did the teacher take Pankaj's eraser?
qa.a: Because he was playing with it.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj feel the whole week was bad?
qa.a: Pankaj still felt upset about Saturday's eraser, and because it was the freshest memory it pushed out Monday's help, the kites and the goal.

qa.q: What choice by Nani helped Pankaj remember more of the week?
qa.a: Asking "And on Monday?" made Pankaj go back day by day, so the earlier good moments could come back into view.

qa.q: How might the maths teacher feel if she knew Pankaj called her mean?
qa.a: She might feel sad or surprised, since she had stayed back to help him with fractions and praised him only days before.

grounding: It shows a boy asked about his week mostly remembering yesterday and judging a teacher by the latest class.

passage:
Class 3 circle-time note, Friday (Alka ma'am)
At our end-of-week circle, I asked each child for one word about the week. Bhupen, 8, said, "Worst." When I asked why, he said PT was cancelled today because of rain. He also said the art teacher is "boring" because yesterday they only coloured.
This was the week of our trip to the planetarium on Tuesday, which he loved; he spent the bus ride explaining black holes to everyone. On Wednesday the same art teacher helped him make a clay rocket that he carried home.
I didn't argue. I put the week's photos on the board in order, Monday to Friday, and asked him to find his favourite. He went straight to the rocket, then the planetarium, and said, "Oh. Tuesday was good."
Next: we will try a "whole week" drawing every Friday, one box for each day.

qa.q: Why was PT cancelled on Friday?
qa.a: PT was cancelled because of rain.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel about his week at first, and what changed?
qa.a: Bhupen felt disappointed about the week because PT was cancelled that day, but looking at the photos he remembered the rocket and planetarium and said, "Oh. Tuesday was good."

qa.q: Which choice by Alka ma'am helped Bhupen, and why?
qa.a: Putting the photos up in order, Monday to Friday, let Bhupen see the earlier days for himself instead of being told he was wrong 🙂

qa.q: How might the art teacher feel hearing Bhupen call the class "boring"?
qa.a: The art teacher might feel disappointed, since just a day earlier they helped Bhupen make a clay rocket he proudly carried home.

grounding: It shows a boy judging his week and a teacher mostly by the last day's events, while earlier good days are crowded out.

passage: Eshaan, you told Mummy your whole week was 'the worst' because of today's argument? Sit with your Hemant dada. When I was nine, my father asked me every Sunday how my week had gone. One Sunday I said, "Terrible. Master-ji is the meanest teacher in the world." Why? Because on Saturday he had made me stand for talking. My father didn't argue. He asked, "And Monday?" On Monday, Master-ji had let me ring the bell. Tuesday, he read us a ghost story. Wednesday, he gave me a star for my map. By Friday I was laughing. "So, one bad Saturday," my father said. I felt a bit foolish, and a bit lighter. After that, whenever anyone asked about my week, I started from Monday.

qa.q: What did Master-ji do on Tuesday?
qa.a: On Tuesday he read the class a ghost story.

qa.q: Why did young Hemant call Master-ji the meanest teacher in the world?
qa.a: Hemant felt hurt and angry about Saturday, and that fresh memory crowded out the good days, so it seemed like the truth about the whole week.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Dada's story?
qa.a: His father asking about each day from Monday, which brought back the bell, the ghost story and the star and showed it was just one bad Saturday.

qa.q: How might Master-ji have felt if he had heard he was called the meanest teacher?
qa.a: Master-ji might have felt hurt or surprised, having given the boy the bell, a story and a star that same week.

grounding: Shows a child judging his teacher and whole week by the most recent day until the earlier days are recalled.

passage: The feedback forms landed on the desks with three minutes left before the bell. "Rate each teacher, one to five," the monitor called. Siddharth scribbled fast. Maths: five, because yesterday's class had a puzzle. PT: one. Yesterday PT sir had cancelled the match for rain and made them sit in the library. Wasim leaned over. "One? He taught us cricket all term. He picked you for the house team." Siddharth's pencil paused. The whole term's matches, the house team, the day sir fixed his bat grip: all of it had been pushed out by one rainy afternoon. The bell was about to ring. He rubbed out the one, wrote a four, and handed the form in just as the monitor grabbed the pile.

qa.q: Why was the match cancelled yesterday?
qa.a: PT sir cancelled the match for rain.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth first give PT sir a one?
qa.a: Siddharth felt annoyed about yesterday's cancelled match, and that fresh disappointment crowded out a whole term of good memories.

qa.q: What helped Siddharth change the rating, and what could he do next time?
qa.a: Wasim's reminder of the cricket and the house team; next time he could think back over the whole term before rating.

qa.q: What would change if Wasim hadn't leaned over?
qa.a: PT sir might have got a one for a single rainy day, despite teaching cricket all term.

grounding: Shows a child judging a teacher by the last class under time pressure until a friend reminds him of the earlier weeks.

passage: At dinner in their Kolkata flat, Payal asked Kiran how his week at Dida's house had been. "Boring," he said, poking his rice. "It rained and I just sat inside." Payal raised her eyebrows. "The whole week?" "Yesterday." "And the day before?" Kiran thought. The day before, Dida had taken him to the river to watch the boats. Before that, he had flown a kite with the neighbour's boys and eaten phuchka twice. On the very first day he had found a kitten under the stairs. His face slowly lit up. "Oh. It was actually good." Payal smiled. "So it wasn't boring?" "Only yesterday was," he said, and went back to his rice, already telling her about the kitten.

qa.q: Where did Kiran spend his week?
qa.a: Kiran spent his week at Dida's house.

qa.q: Why did Kiran first say the week was boring?
qa.a: Kiran felt bored and a bit glum about yesterday's rain, and that latest day crowded out the river, the kite and the kitten.

qa.q: How did Payal help Kiran remember the whole week?
qa.a: She asked about the day before, and the day before that, walking back through the week instead of accepting one word.

qa.q: How might Dida feel if she heard the week called boring?
qa.a: Dida might feel hurt or disappointed, having taken Kiran to the river and watched him find the kitten.

grounding: Shows a child judging a whole week by yesterday's rainy day until he is asked about the earlier days.

passage: When Papa asked me on Saturday about my week, I said it was terrible. I'm Tejas, and I really believed it. On Friday I got a low mark in the dictation, and our class teacher had been cross all day. So I told him the teacher was mean and the week was the worst. Papa took out the diary where I write one line every day. Monday: "Won the kabaddi match." Tuesday: "Teacher let us go early." Wednesday: "Teacher praised my map." Thursday: "Made a new friend." Friday: "Bad dictation." I felt funny reading it. Four good days, one bad. And the teacher I called mean had praised my map two days before. Now I read my diary before I answer Papa.

qa.q: What did Tejas write in the diary on Wednesday?
qa.a: "Teacher praised my map."

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when reading the diary?
qa.a: Tejas felt funny and a bit embarrassed, seeing four good days that had been forgotten because Friday came last.

qa.q: What does Tejas do now, and why does it help?
qa.a: Tejas reads the diary before answering Papa, so the whole week counts, not just the most recent day.

qa.q: How might Papa see Tejas's "worst week"?
qa.a: Papa seems to suspect it was not so bad, which is why he took out the diary to check.

grounding: A child looks back on calling a week terrible and a teacher mean because of the last day, until a daily diary shows the rest.

passage:
Class 3 observation note, Friday.
In circle time I asked children to describe their week in one word. Akash said "boring." When I asked why, he said the drawing class this morning was boring and the teacher was boring. I reminded him that on Tuesday he had told me drawing was his favourite, and on Wednesday he'd made a rocket everyone admired. He looked surprised, as if those days had disappeared.
Several children did the same thing: the week was whatever happened last.
Next week I will try a small change. Each afternoon, the children will draw one picture of the best thing that day in a small "week book." On Friday, they will look through the whole book before choosing their word.
Disha

qa.q: What word did Akash use to describe his week?
qa.a: Boring.

qa.q: What does Akash's surprise suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He seemed puzzled and a bit sheepish, as if Tuesday and Wednesday had vanished, because the boring morning felt like the whole week.

qa.q: What is the teacher's plan, and why might it help?
qa.a: A daily "week book" picture of the best thing, reviewed on Friday, so children remember the whole week and not just the last day.

qa.q: How might the drawing teacher feel hearing Akash call the class boring?
qa.a: The drawing teacher might feel disappointed, not knowing Akash loved the class earlier that week.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child judging his week and a class by the most recent morning, forgetting earlier good days.

passage:
Friday, last day before the Christmas holidays.
Dear diary, Mummy asked how my week was. I said "boring and bad", because today Vidya Ma'am gave us a surprise test and didn't let us go to the Christmas party early. She is the strictest teacher ever.
Then Mummy looked at my school diary. On Monday Vidya Ma'am gave me a star for my story. On Tuesday we made paper snowflakes in her class. On Wednesday she let me read aloud. On Thursday she brought plum cake for everyone.
I forgot all that. I only remembered today.
Okay, maybe my week was good and only today was bad. Maybe Vidya Ma'am is nice and only strict on Fridays.
Tushar

qa.a: Vidya Ma'am brought plum cake for everyone on Thursday.

qa.a: Tushar felt cross and disappointed about today's surprise test, and that fresh feeling crowded out the good days earlier in the week.

qa.q: What helped Tushar remember the whole week?
qa.a: Looking at the school diary with Mummy brought back Monday's star, Tuesday's snowflakes, Wednesday's reading and Thursday's cake.

qa.q: How might Vidya Ma'am feel if she heard she was 'the strictest teacher ever'?
qa.a: Vidya Ma'am might feel hurt or surprised, having given stars, crafts and cake all week.

grounding: Shows a child who judges a whole week and a teacher by the last day, until earlier events are brought back.

passage:
It was mustard season, and the fields outside the village school glowed yellow. At dinner, Madhav's grandfather asked, "So, how is the new teacher, Dilnaz Madam?"
"Very bad," Madhav said at once. "Yesterday she made me stand because I didn't finish my sums."
"And before yesterday?"
Madhav chewed his roti. Before yesterday felt far away. Slowly he remembered: on the first day she taught them a song about the monsoon. On Thursday she took them out to the mustard fields to count bees. On Friday she let him ring the bell.
"She's... okay," he said. "Mostly nice. Yesterday was bad."
His grandfather nodded. "One day is not a person."

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz Madam take the class on Thursday?
qa.a: She took them out to the mustard fields to count bees.

qa.q: Why did Madhav say the teacher was very bad?
qa.a: Madhav still felt upset and embarrassed about standing yesterday, and that fresh memory pushed out the good days.

qa.q: What question from the grandfather helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking 'And before yesterday?' made Madhav recall the song, the bee counting and the bell, so the whole week counted.

qa.q: How does Madhav's grandfather see the new teacher?
qa.a: The grandfather keeps an open mind, reminding Madhav that one day is not a person.

grounding: Shows a child who judges a new teacher by yesterday's class, forgetting the better days before it.

passage:
On the last day of the summer term in Manchester, Kwame's mum asked in the car, "So how was Year 6, all in all?"
"Rubbish," Kwame said. "We lost the final match on Tuesday. Five-nil."
Rania, squashed in the back seat because she lived on the same road, leaned forward. "Kwame. You won the science fair in October."
"Oh. Yeah."
"And you were the wolf in the school play. Everybody laughed."
"That was ages ago."
"And we went to the seaside in May and you found that crab."
Kwame looked out of the window. The five-nil still felt like the loudest thing. But the crab was coming back to him, and the wolf costume with the ears.
"Maybe it was a good year," he said, "with a bad Tuesday."

qa.q: What was the score in the final match?
qa.a: They lost the final match five-nil on Tuesday.

qa.q: Why did Kwame call Year 6 rubbish?
qa.a: Kwame still felt disappointed about Tuesday's loss, and that recent feeling crowded out the whole year.

qa.q: What did Rania do that helped Kwame see the year fairly?
qa.a: Rania listed earlier moments, the science fair, the wolf part and the crab at the seaside, bringing the whole year back.

qa.q: How does Rania remember Year 6?
qa.a: Rania remembers it as full of Kwame's good moments and wants him to see them too.

grounding: Shows a child who judges a whole school year by its last disappointing week until earlier moments are recalled.

passage: Sunday was phone day at the boarding school, the week after Holi. Sachin sat in the warden's office with the heavy black phone. "How was your week, beta?" Papa asked. Sachin thought hard. "Terrible. Uday sir made us run four rounds yesterday because we were late. He's the strictest teacher ever." "Warden uncle told me Uday sir taught you to swim this week." "That was ages ago." It had been Tuesday. On Wednesday Uday sir had shared his own gujiya with the whole dorm, and on Thursday he had stayed late to help Sachin fix his kite. But all Sachin could feel were the four rounds, still aching in his legs. "The week was bad, Papa," he said. "Really bad."

qa.a: Four rounds, yesterday, because they were late.

qa.q: Why does Sachin call the whole week terrible?
qa.a: Yesterday's four rounds are the freshest memory and still ache, so Sachin feels grumpy and sure the week was bad, crowding out the swimming, the gujiya and the kite.

qa.q: What could Papa ask to help Sachin remember the whole week?
qa.a: He could go day by day, asking what happened on Monday, Tuesday and so on, so the earlier good moments come back.

qa.q: How might Uday sir feel if he heard himself called the strictest teacher ever?
qa.a: Uday sir might feel a little hurt or amused, having taught Sachin to swim, shared his gujiya and helped fix the kite that same week 😅
